scenario: A family wants to replace a drawer full of old chargers and cables. Most of the newer gear uses the same reversible USB-C connector, but one phone charges much more slowly on one brick than on its original charger, two similar-looking cables behave differently, and adding a second device can change charging speed. The available material includes ULTRANET and ALOGIC multiport charger listings; one USB-C cable listing that claims 100 W, 20 Gbit/s, an e-marker, and conditional video; another that claims 60 W and USB 2.0 data; several phone-owner troubleshooting threads; and background pages about USB history, negotiation, Galaxy S22 family charging profiles, and the Realme GT Neo5 proprietary charging bundle.
target: Explain why the industry converged on USB-C while identical-looking chargers and cables can still behave differently. Use the named charger and cable listings, the Galaxy S22 and Realme GT Neo5 examples, and the owner reports to trace the connector, protocol, charger-port, phone-profile, cable, and device-state layers. Then give the family a conditional consolidation plan. The table should record each exact phone, brick, selected port, other-port occupancy, cable power or current, data generation, e-marker and alternate-mode limits, and relevant phone documentation. The controlled check should hold starting battery range, temperature, phone activity, elapsed time, and other-port use steady, then log negotiated mode when observable, battery change, measured power when suitable equipment is available, temperature, disconnects, data or video behavior, and the effect of adding another device. State clearly what one exact test can establish and what the available evidence cannot establish about universal speed or long-term reliability.
